column11: Area with dense, evergreen forest cover dominated by mangrove species, occurring in intertidal zones, river mouths, and estuaries, adapted to shallow brackish waters, with specific adaptations to grow on flat, muddy soils. Mangroves from the genera Rhizophora, Avicennia, Conocarpus, and Laguncularia are predominant.
Area with predominantly tree-covered natural vegetation, seasonally or permanently flooded, located in zones adjacent to water bodies and floodplains, subject to periods of inundation.

Areas of vegetation predominantly composed of native herbaceous species (grass) or natural tropical grasslands. This includes Deciduous Herbaceous Cover and Deciduous Herbaceous Cover at Altitude (arid zones located mainly in the high parts of the volcanic cones on Isabela Island).

Geological mass that emerges at the Earth's surface, covering extensive areas with rocky materials of various sizes. This category includes scars left by eruptive processes, lahars, and sand fields. In the Galápagos biome, it includes areas of both ancient and recent lava flows. In the Andes biome, this class is generally found above 4,000 meters above sea level, where the subalpine, alpine, and nival altitudinal zones are located—areas characterized by sparse or absent vegetation.

Areas of vegetation predominantly composed of native herbaceous species (grasses) or natural tropical Andean grasslands that grow above the tree line (approximately 3000-3500 m elevation). These grasslands become more scattered as altitude increases and are not subject to flooding periods. This cover is primarily constituted by the so-called "páramos de pajonal," whose height does not exceed 2 meters. They consist of mosaics of species, with the main components being grasses from the genera Festuca and Calamagrostis, and herbs from the genera Gentianella, Senecio, Huperzia, and Oritophium. They may also include scattered arboreal or shrubby elements.

Areas of vegetation composed of native andean herbaceous species that form in areas where the soil maintains perennially anaerobic conditions, limiting the decomposition of organic matter and promoting the accumulation of deep organic soils. They may or may not be covered by a water sheet. In some locations, they are dominated by species that form cushions or pads that do not exceed heights of 50 cm (Distichia spp., Plantago rigida, Disterigma empetrifolium, Oreobus ecuadoriensis), or by mosaics of herbaceous species and mosses. These formations occur at high altitudes (approximately 3000-3500 m elevation). This vegetation is primarily constituted by so-called flooded páramos, wetlands, hygrophilous peatlands, or bofedales

Forest mass artificially established with one or more native or introduced timber species, all of the same age, evenly spaced, managed through silvicultural practices, and intended for various purposes such as timber production, protection, soil restoration, or recreation. Pine forests of the species Pinus patula and Pinus radiata have been established for reforestation and timber exploitation purposes.

Areas where the natural cover has been modified, removed, or replaced by other types of vegetation cover for agricultural or livestock use, and where cultivated species are grouped for the production of food, fibers, or pastures. These areas occur in a mosaic pattern and therefore cannot be individually distinguished; exceptionally, they may be associated with fallow land or successional natural vegetation.

Perennial crop, mainly Musa × paradisiaca, which belongs to the Musaceae family. It is a herbaceous plant that can reach up to 7.5 meters in height and is found primarily on the Ecuadorian coast, where the tropical climate and humidity favor its growth. Several varieties of banana and plantain are considered, produced mainly in large-scale commercial plantations almost exclusively dedicated to export.

Coastal and riparian areas formed by the action of waves and currents, where the soil ranges from fine and coarse sands to pebbles or gravel, and may support sparse vegetation adapted to salinity and moisture. This includes dunes, sandbanks, and beaches of water bodies, characterized by loose sandy soils and minimal vegetation.

Human settlement area associated with large and small urban centers (towns), with built environment infrastructure such as road and railway networks and associated land, as well as other artificialized zones like hydrocarbon extraction sites, hydroelectric plants, military bases, airports, ports, and unconventional airstrips in rural areas. Peripheral areas undergoing a gradual process of urbanization for residential and/or industrial purposes are also included.

Areas with little or no vegetation, of anthropogenic origin, not mapped under other classes. These may include transitional crop areas, roads and highways, airstrips, industrial yards, and recently deforested zones.

Surface areas used for the extraction of rock or mineral materials, with clear soil exposure. No distinction is made regarding whether the activity is industrial or artisanal, legal or illegal, or whether the materials are metallic or non-metallic. Most of the extraction is alluvial and not carried out in underground mines.

Areas with poorly developed soils and sparse or nonexistent vegetation, formed by natural geological and climatic processes. This includes high-altitude deserts, arid zones, and areas affected by landslides, characterized by sandy or rocky soils. These areas may have very scattered vegetation adapted to extreme edaphic and climatic conditions.
Extent of artificial surface water bodies dedicated to productive activities, such as saltwater ponds for captive shrimp farming or freshwater ponds for fish farming.
Extent of natural or artificial surface water. Includes rivers, lakes, reservoirs, and other bodies of water.
Area of permanent ice cover or mass, located on Andean summits, resulting from the accumulation, compaction, and recrystallization of snow.
